These newborns, weighing roughly 1,800,000 grams [Wwb = roughly 1,800,000 grams], are immediately capable of swimming alongside their mothers in the cold, productive waters of the world's oceans. This substantial neonatal mass is essential for thermoregulation and sustained swimming effort during the early dependence phase. The mother-calf bond is intensive, with the calf relying entirely on lipid-rich milk for its rapid somatic development. The duration of this nutritional dependency, measured from birth to the cessation of suckling, has been documented at approximately 183 days from birth [tx = approximately 183 days from birth] under the endothermic conditions typical of this species, with a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This weaning period aligns with the seasonal migration patterns that characterize the species, allowing the calf to gain significant condition before undertaking its first independent northward feeding journey. The transition to independent feeding marks a critical threshold in the calf's life history, as it must then locate and capture dense aggregations of krill to sustain its massive energy requirements.

Sexual maturation in fin whales is a protracted process, with the two sexes exhibiting distinct timelines for the attainment of puberty. The length at which females typically achieve this developmental milestone is roughly 18.3 meters [Lp = roughly 18.3 meters], although field observations indicate that the range can extend from 17.7 meters up to 19 meters depending on nutritional history and individual variation. Attaining this body size is a prerequisite for successfully carrying a foetus to term within the energetic constraints imposed by the marine environment.

This modest output represents a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward offspring survival rather than numerical productivity, a common pattern among large-bodied mammals that invest considerable maternal resources in each single calf. The gestation period itself, from conception to live birth, lasts 342 days [tg = 342 days] at the species' core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a duration that is consistent with the prolonged organogenesis and foetal growth required to deliver a precocial offspring of such massive proportions. After this gestation period, the newborn emerges ready for immediate aquatic locomotion, a stark contrast to the altricial neonates of many terrestrial mammals. This extended pregnancy is followed by the weaning period of roughly six months, during which the calf nearly doubles its birth length.

Adult body size in Balaenoptera physalus exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining considerably larger ultimate lengths than their male counterparts. The maximum recorded adult length for females reaches 20.5 meters [Li = 20.5 meters], placing them among the longest of the rorqual whales. Males, in contrast, achieve a slightly smaller ultimate length of approximately 19.2 meters [Li = approximately 19.2 meters]. This pattern of female-biased size dimorphism is believed to be driven by the selective pressures of reproductive energetics, as larger body size in females provides greater capacity for lipid storage to buffer the immense costs of gestation and lactation over the prolonged calving intervals. The somatic growth trajectory that leads to these terminal dimensions is remarkably steep during the first several years of life, with calves rapidly attaining lengths of 12 meters within their first year. As they approach their maximum size, growth slows considerably, with energy being increasingly diverted toward maintenance rather than structural increase.

Longevity in this species, as estimated from bomb-lance marks in earplugs and from mark-recapture studies of known individuals, suggests a maximum lifespan of approximately 114 years [am = approximately 114 years] under the physiological temperature conditions of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] that are standard for this endotherm. This remarkable lifespan, among the longest documented for any cetacean, underscores a life-history strategy defined by extreme iteroparity, where a female may produce only a handful of calves over a reproductive career spanning many decades. The very low reproductive rate, combined with delayed maturity and extreme longevity, renders the fin whale highly vulnerable to perturbations in adult survival, a key consideration for its conservation status. Current population recovery from historical whaling remains slow precisely because of these demographic constraints, with even small increases in mortality from ship strikes or entanglement disproportionately impacting population growth rates. The species thus represents an archetype of a slow life-history pace, where survival of each individual adult is paramount for population persistence.
